title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
contentHtml:
Political commentators have been obsessed with potential polling error this cycle. And frankly, with the combination of recent high-profile misses and polls looking increasingly like mini-models, it’s hard to blame them. We’ve also covered the topic in some detail, and it can be especially concerning for forecasters when Democrats are putting up their best polling performances in traditionally red states. Some analysts are predicting that the polls will overestimate Democrats as they have in the past few presidential elections: Republican voters can be hard to reach. However, there are also credible arguments for why they could just as easily be underrating Democrats.

We think it’s usually a bad idea to try and predict the direction of polling error a priori. But in general, people are hesitant to take the polls at face value this year. In part, that might be because the polls at face value are excellent for Democrats. They lead by 8.9 points in our generic ballot average — that’s a 0.9-point larger lead than they had at this point in 2018. Applying FLIPR’s likely voter adjustment further boosts that lead to D +9.2.

Their recent state-level polls are, if anything, even better.

We mostly write about our “Deluxe” forecast that incorporates fundamentals and expert ratings, but here’s FLIPR’s “Lite” (polls only) Senate forecast. Using the polls alone, FLIPR expects Democrats to easily flip North Carolina, and have about a 75 percent shot in Texas, Ohio, Maine, and (most surprisingly) Kansas. Alaska (63 percent) and Iowa (56 percent) are tougher Democratic flips, while Abdul El-Sayed has an 85 percent chance of holding the Michigan Senate seat — and it’s unlikely the Haley Stevens debacle will change that number.
